Reactions to Stress","kind":"detailed_source_grounded_notes","printedStart":376,"printedEnd":382,"pdfStart":394,"pdfEnd":400,"content":[{"type":"paragraph","text":"Stress influences both emotional experience and bodily function. The general adaptation syndrome and the hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal axis describe important components of the physiological stress response."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The book also considers the immune system, the enteric nervous system, and coping. Follow how a temporary response may differ from the effects of persistent stress."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m11-3-study-1","text":"Stress as an adaptive response"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Stress arises when an organism faces demands or threats requiring adjustment. The general adaptation syndrome describes a broad pattern of bodily response that changes over time. In an acute challenge, physiological activation may support attention and action. Prolonged activation, however, can contribute to wear on bodily systems. Whether a particular demand is harmful depends on intensity, duration, resources, and interpretation, not simply the presence of a measurable stress hormone."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m11-3-study-2","text":"The hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal axis"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The HPA axis links brain signals to endocrine activity. Hypothalamic signaling influences the pituitary, which in turn influences adrenal cortex secretion of glucocorticoids such as cortisol. This helps organize metabolic and other responses to challenge. Feedback mechanisms regulate the system, and its time course differs from faster autonomic responses. A useful revision skill is to trace the sequence of glands and signals without mixing it up with the sympathetic nervous system."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m11-3-study-3","text":"Stress and immunity"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Immune processes interact with nervous and endocrine systems. Stress can influence immune activity, and its effects differ across acute versus prolonged circumstances and across immune outcomes. These connections do not mean stress is the sole cause of infection or illness. The enteric nervous system and gut-related communication provide additional routes linking bodily states with behavior. Biological evidence should be interpreted in context rather than reduced to the slogan that stress 'weakens everything'."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m11-3-study-4","text":"Coping and regulation"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Coping strategies can change exposure to a stressor, a person's interpretation, or the bodily consequences of ongoing strain. Social support, controllability, and circumstances matter. The best way to study stress is to connect three levels: the demanding event, the brain–hormone–immune processes it recruits, and the person's behavioral response. Different interventions act at different levels, which is why no single coping technique solves every problem."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-3-h01","text":"Stress and the General Adaptation Syndrome"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Hans Selye popularized the concept of stress , defining it as the nonspecific response of the body to any demand made upon it.","sourcePrintedPage":376,"sourcePdfPage":394,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Selye inferred that any threat activated a generalized response, which he called the general adaptation syndrome .","sourcePrintedPage":376,"sourcePdfPage":394,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In the initial stage, which he called alarm, the sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for brief emergency activity.","sourcePrintedPage":376,"sourcePdfPage":394,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The anterior pituitary gland secretes adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) , which stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete glucocorticoid hormones, mainly cortisol in humans.","sourcePrintedPage":376,"sourcePdfPage":394,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The HPA axis reacts to stress more gradually than the sympathetic nervous system, but its effects continue as long as the stress continues.","sourcePrintedPage":376,"sourcePdfPage":394,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After intense, prolonged stress, the body enters the third stage, exhaustion , when the nervous and immune systems no longer have the energy to sustain their responses.","sourcePrintedPage":376,"sourcePdfPage":394,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Stress-related illnesses and psychiatric problems are widespread in industrial societies, possibly because of changes in the type of stresses we face.","sourcePrintedPage":376,"sourcePdfPage":394,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Selye’s concept of stress included any change in one’s life, including both favorable and unfavorable events.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Still, as Jerome Kagan observed, researchers’ concepts of stress have ranged from life-threatening events to matters of brief inconvenience.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-3-h02","text":"Stress and the Hypothalamus-Pituitary-Adrenal Cortex Axis"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Stress can impair health indirectly by altering people’s behaviors.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Widows and widowers have a greatly increased risk of heart attack or stroke for the next several months , largely because they tend to eat worse meals, consume more alcohol, sleep less, and exercise less than previously .","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Stress also alters nervous system activity in ways that impair health.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Brief or moderate stress improves energetic performance, vigilance, and memory formation, especially for learning fears .","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Brief stress enhances activity of the immune system, helping it fight illnesses, but prolonged stress impairs immune activity and memory .","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-3-h03","text":"The Immune System"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The immune system consists of cells that protect the body against viruses, bacteria, and other intruders.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The immune system is like a police force: If it is too weak, the criminals (viruses and bacteria) run wild and create damage.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If it becomes too strong, it might start attacking law-abiding citizens (the body’s own cells).","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When the immune system attacks normal cells, we call the result an autoimmune","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The primary components of the immune system are the leukocytes , commonly known as white blood cells.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In response to an infection, leukocytes and other cells produce small proteins called cytokines (e.g., interleukin-1, or IL-1) that combat infections.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Cytokines fight the illness, but when cytokine levels get too high, they produce nasal congestion, a runny nose, and other symptoms associated with illness.","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sleep and inactivity conserve energy so that the body can devote more energy to its immune attack against the intruders .","sourcePrintedPage":377,"sourcePdfPage":395,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-3-h04","text":"Effects of Stress on the Immune System"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The nervous system has more control than we might have guessed over the immune system.","sourcePrintedPage":378,"sourcePdfPage":396,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The study of this relationship, called psychoneuroimmunology , deals with how experiences alter the immune system and how the immune system in turn influences the central nervous system.","sourcePrintedPage":378,"sourcePdfPage":396,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In response to a brief stressful experience, the nervous system activates the immune system to produce more natural killer cells and cytokines.","sourcePrintedPage":378,"sourcePdfPage":396,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cytokines help combat infections that might result from an injury, and they also trigger prostaglandins that reach the hypothalamus, where they produce the same effects as an illness—sleepiness, decreased appetite, and elevated body temperature .","sourcePrintedPage":378,"sourcePdfPage":396,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Even viewing extremely disgusting images can activate the immune system and raise body temperature .","sourcePrintedPage":378,"sourcePdfPage":396,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A prolonged stress response produces symptoms of depression and weakens the immune system .","sourcePrintedPage":378,"sourcePdfPage":396,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A study of research scientists in Antarctica found that a 9-month period of cold, darkness, and social isolation reduced T cell functioning to about half of normal levels .","sourcePrintedPage":378,"sourcePdfPage":396,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Brief or mild levels of stress produces cortisol that puts the brakes on excess cytokines that produce symptoms of illness, but after prolonged stress, the body becomes less responsive to cortisol and the inflammation continues unabated.","sourcePrintedPage":378,"sourcePdfPage":396,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-3-h05","text":"The Role of the Enteric Nervous System"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When you experience stress, you notice stomach churning, diarrhea, and other signs of digestive upset.","sourcePrintedPage":379,"sourcePdfPage":397,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"These are products of the enteric nervous system , a set of neurons that control digestion, stretching from the esophagus to the rectum.","sourcePrintedPage":379,"sourcePdfPage":397,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The enteric system reacts to stress because of input from the brain and from the hormones released by stress.","sourcePrintedPage":379,"sourcePdfPage":397,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most of those bacteria are helpful, but some produce irritable bowel syndrome and visceral pain, and some produce chemicals that increase the risk of anxiety and depression .","sourcePrintedPage":379,"sourcePdfPage":397,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Your reaction to stress depends on what happens throughout your body, not just what happens in your brain.","sourcePrintedPage":379,"sourcePdfPage":397,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m11-3-h06","text":"Coping with Stress"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People vary in their reactions to a stressful experience because of both genetic predispositions and previous experiences.","sourcePrintedPage":379,"sourcePdfPage":397,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Resilience —the ability to recover well from a traumatic The general adaptation syndrome describes a broad pattern of bodily response that changes over time. In an acute challenge, physiological activation may support attention and action. Prolonged activation, however, can contribute to wear on bodily systems. Whether a particular demand is harmful depends on intensity, duration, resources, and interpretation, not simply the presence of a measurable stress hormone.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":376,"sourcePrintedEnd":382,"sourcePdfStart":394,"sourcePdfEnd":400},{"id":"bp14-m11-3-study-2","title":"The hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal axis","text":"The HPA axis links brain signals to endocrine activity. Hypothalamic signaling influences the pituitary, which in turn influences adrenal cortex secretion of glucocorticoids such as cortisol. This helps organize metabolic and other responses to challenge. Feedback mechanisms regulate the system, and its time course differs from faster autonomic responses. These reactions can be adaptive in the short term and costly when sustained. A comprehensive account of stress connects appraisal and behavior to the neural and physiological mechanisms that follow.","paragraphIndex":803006,"kind":"individually_written_classroom_explanation","level":"contextual_clarification","sourceHeadingId":"bp14-m11-3-h07","sourcePrintedPage":379,"sourcePdfPage":397,"editorialStatus":"individual_topic_specific_explanation_drafted_from_source_topic_map","evidenceBasis":"Supplied Kalat 14e PDF and matching Markdown; existing source-extracted paragraphs kept as separate verifiable references","needsIndependentReview":true}}],"classroomParagraphs":["Hans Selye popularized the concept of stress, defining it as the nonspecific response of the body to any demand made upon it.","Selye inferred that any threat activated a generalized response, which he called the general adaptation syndrome.","In the initial stage, which he called alarm, the sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for brief emergency activity.","The anterior pituitary gland secretes adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete glucocorticoid hormones, mainly cortisol in humans. The HPA axis reacts to stress more gradually than the sympathetic nervous system, but its effects continue as long as the stress continues.","After intense, prolonged stress, the body enters the third stage, exhaustion, when the nervous and immune systems no longer have the energy to sustain their responses.","Stress-related illnesses and psychiatric problems are widespread in industrial societies, possibly because of changes in the type of stresses we face. Selye’s concept of stress included any change in one’s life, including both favorable and unfavorable events.","Still, as Jerome Kagan observed, researchers’ concepts of stress have ranged from life-threatening events to matters of brief inconvenience.","Stress can impair health indirectly by altering people’s behaviors.","Widows and widowers have a greatly increased risk of heart attack or stroke for the next several months, largely because they tend to eat worse meals, consume more alcohol, sleep less, and exercise less than previously.","Stress also alters nervous system activity in ways that impair health. Brief or moderate stress improves energetic performance, vigilance, and memory formation, especially for learning fears.","Brief stress enhances activity of the immune system, helping it fight illnesses, but prolonged stress impairs immune activity and memory.","The immune system consists of cells that protect the body against viruses, bacteria, and other intruders.","The immune system is like a police force: If it is too weak, the criminals (viruses and bacteria) run wild and create damage.","If it becomes too strong, it might start attacking law-abiding citizens (the body’s own cells). When the immune system attacks normal cells, we call the result an autoimmune","The primary components of the immune system are the leukocytes, commonly known as white blood cells.","In response to an infection, leukocytes and other cells produce small proteins called cytokines (e.g., interleukin-1, or IL-1) that combat infections.","Cytokines fight the illness, but when cytokine levels get too high, they produce nasal congestion, a runny nose, and other symptoms associated with illness. Sleep and inactivity conserve energy so that the body can devote more energy to its immune attack against the intruders.","The nervous system has more control than we might have guessed over the immune system.","The study of this relationship, called psychoneuroimmunology, deals with how experiences alter the immune system and how the immune system in turn influences the central nervous system.","In response to a brief stressful experience, the nervous system activates the immune system to produce more natural killer cells and cytokines. The cytokines help combat infections that might result from an injury, and they also trigger prostaglandins that reach the hypothalamus, where they produce the same effects as an illness—sleepiness, decreased appetite, and elevated body temperature.","Even viewing extremely disgusting images can activate the immune system and raise body temperature.","A prolonged stress response produces symptoms of depression and weakens the immune system.","A study of research scientists in Antarctica found that a 9-month period of cold, darkness, and social isolation reduced T cell functioning to about half of normal levels. Brief or mild levels of stress produces cortisol that puts the brakes on excess cytokines that produce symptoms of illness, but after prolonged stress, the body becomes less responsive to cortisol and the inflammation continues unabated.","When you experience stress, you notice stomach churning, diarrhea, and other signs of digestive upset.","These are products of the enteric nervous system, a set of neurons that control digestion, stretching from the esophagus to the rectum.","The enteric system reacts to stress because of input from the brain and from the hormones released by stress. Most of those bacteria are helpful, but some produce irritable bowel syndrome and visceral pain, and some produce chemicals that increase the risk of anxiety and depression.","Your reaction to stress depends on what happens throughout your body, not just what happens in your brain.","Coping with stress involves both physiological regulation and social or behavioral resources. Although stress reactions can help in an immediate challenge, prolonged stress may impair health, memory, and flexible behavior.","People with reliable social relationships often show lower distress. In a study discussed by Kalat, holding a spouse’s hand during painful stimulation reduced neural responses in several brain regions.","Decades ago, Hans Selye argued that any stressful event leads to the general adaptation syndrome, marked by fever and other signs of illness.","We now see why: The body reacts to prolonged stress by activating the adrenal cortex and the immune system, and the resulting increase in","Those factors in turn correlate with the ability to rapidly activate the stress response and then rapidly deactivate it.","Holding the husband’s hand reduced the response indicated by fMRI in several brain areas, including the prefrontal cortex. As predicted, the brain responses corresponded to people’s self-reports that social support from a loved one helps reduce stress.","The organization in the best position to do such a study is the military.","Kalat emphasizes social support and resilience. These findings do not imply that one technique removes stress; they show that stress responses vary with relationships, past experiences, and the situation.","Research following people through stressful experiences links greater distress to factors such as earlier trauma, concussions, mental-health difficulties, and limited close social relationships.","Stress has biological effects as well as psychological meanings. Coping strategies can change exposure to stressors or the degree of support available during them.","Sustained stress-related hormonal activity can affect the hippocampus and other bodily systems. simple mechanism. Research on the engram has changed over time, and psychologists distinguish working, short-term, and long-term memory."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The module also examines consolidation, Alzheimer’s disease, and infant amnesia. Separate the loss of stored information from difficulty creating or accessing memories when comparing examples of memory impairment."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-1-study-1","text":"Memory is not one storage box"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Learning can change behavior, but memory includes several kinds of information and different neural processes. Short-term retention, working memory, and long-term remembering differ in duration and functional demands. Working memory involves actively maintaining and using information for a current task. Long-term memory includes different forms, such as recalling events or gradually acquiring skills. The possibility that someone can lose one kind of memory while retaining another shows why the word 'memory' should not be treated as a single ability."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-1-study-2","text":"The search for where memories are stored"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Early researchers, including Lashley, investigated whether memories occupy sharply localized brain sites. Results challenged the view that one tiny cortical location contains an entire learned response. Modern approaches investigate distributed neuronal populations and the ways training changes their connectivity. An engram refers to the physical changes underlying a memory, but identifying neurons active during learning is not by itself proof that they constitute the whole memory. Representations may involve several brain regions and time-dependent changes."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-1-study-3","text":"Consolidation and forgetting"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Memories can change after initial learning through consolidation, retrieval, and reconsolidation-related processes. This means the formation of a lasting memory is not simply a one-time filing operation. Forgetting can arise through different mechanisms, including disrupted acquisition, storage, or retrieval. Stress, context, and brain damage may affect these processes differently. When interpreting a memory test, ask what type of learning was required and whether the person could express the information in another way."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m12-1-study-4","text":"Clinical patterns"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Alzheimer's disease is associated with progressive changes in cognitive function and neural pathology, but memory difficulties alone do not establish that diagnosis. Infant amnesia refers to the limited ability adults have to recall early childhood autobiographical episodes; it does not mean infants are incapable of learning. Such examples demonstrate that memory is constrained by brain development, neural health, and the kind of information being assessed."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-1-h01","text":"Localized Representations of Memory"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The experimenter presents a conditioned stimulus (CS) that initially elicits no response of note, and then presents the unconditioned stimulus (UCS) that automatically elicits the unconditioned response (UCR) .","sourcePrintedPage":384,"sourcePdfPage":402,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After some pairings of the CS and the UCS (perhaps just one or two, perhaps many), the individual begins making a new response to the CS, called a conditioned response (CR) .","sourcePrintedPage":384,"sourcePdfPage":402,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In his original experiments, Pavlov presented a dog with a sound (CS) followed by meat (UCS), which stimulated the dog to salivate (UCR).","sourcePrintedPage":384,"sourcePdfPage":402,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A reinforcer increases the future probability of the response, and a punishment suppresses the frequency.","sourcePrintedPage":384,"sourcePdfPage":402,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For example, when a rat enters one arm of a maze and finds Froot Loops cereal (a treat that rats seem to love), the rat increases its probability of entering that arm at future opportunities.","sourcePrintedPage":384,"sourcePdfPage":402,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The primary difference between classical and instrumental conditioning is that in instrumental conditioning the individual’s response determines the outcome (reinforcer or punishment), whereas in classical conditioning the","sourcePrintedPage":384,"sourcePdfPage":402,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For example, after a male songbird hears the song of his own species during his first few months, he imitates it the following year.","sourcePrintedPage":386,"sourcePdfPage":404,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-1-h02","text":"Lashley’s Search for the Engram"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, psychologists of an earlier era were unaware of such observations and considered Pavlov’s hypothesis plausible.","sourcePrintedPage":386,"sourcePdfPage":404,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Karl Lashley set out to test it, searching for the engram — the physical representation of what has been learned.","sourcePrintedPage":386,"sourcePdfPage":404,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A connection between two brain areas would be a possible example of an engram.","sourcePrintedPage":386,"sourcePdfPage":404,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Lashley reasoned that if learning depends on new or strengthened connections between brain areas, a knife cut somewhere in the brain should interrupt that connection and abolish the learned response.","sourcePrintedPage":386,"sourcePdfPage":404,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because neither of these tasks is a case of classical conditioning, they were not ideal ways to test Pavlov’s theory.","sourcePrintedPage":386,"sourcePdfPage":404,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Lashley also tested whether any portion of the cerebral cortex is more important than others for learning.","sourcePrintedPage":386,"sourcePdfPage":404,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Eventually, researchers found that Lashley’s conclusions rested on unnecessary assumptions: (a) that the cerebral cortex is the best or only place to search for an engram and (b) that studying one example of learning is just as good as studying any other one.","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-1-h03","text":"The Modern Search for the Engram"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Thompson and his colleagues used a simpler task than Lashley’s and sought the engram in the cerebellum instead of the cerebral cortex.","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"They presented first a tone (CS) and then a puff of air (UCS) to the cornea of the rabbit’s eye.","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If area E were temporarily blocked, nothing would relay information to the muscles, so we would see no response, but learning could occur nevertheless, and we could see evidence of it later.","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Thompson’s research identified one nucleus of the cerebellum, the lateral interpositus nucleus (LIP) , as essential for learning.","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In the next experiments, investigators temporarily suppressed activity in the red nucleus, a midbrain motor area that receives input from the cerebellum.","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, after the red nucleus had recovered, the rabbits immediately exhibited strong learned responses to the tone .","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This research made it possible for other researchers to explore the mechanisms in more detail, identifying the cells and neurotransmitters responsible for this example of an engram .","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, they report that they know the stimulus predicts a puff of air to the eyes, and they do exhibit a classically conditioned change in skin conductance .","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-1-h04","text":"Types of Memory"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Finding an engram for certain types of classical conditioning is an important accomplishment, but finding an engram for everyday memories is more challenging.","sourcePrintedPage":388,"sourcePdfPage":406,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"much of the 20th century, most psychologists assumed that all memory was the same.","sourcePrintedPage":388,"sourcePdfPage":406,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If so, they could study it with any convenient example, such as memorizing nonsense syllables, just as physicists can measure gravity by dropping any convenient object.","sourcePrintedPage":388,"sourcePdfPage":406,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Eventually, psychologists recognized differences among types of memory.","sourcePrintedPage":388,"sourcePdfPage":406,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-1-h05","text":"Short-Term and Long-Term Memory"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Donald Hebb reasoned that no one mechanism could account for all the phenomena of learning.","sourcePrintedPage":388,"sourcePdfPage":406,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"between short-term memory of events that have just occurred and long-term memory of events from further back.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Hebb suggested that we might store short-term memories by a reverberating circuit, in which neuron A excites neuron B, which excites neuron C, which then reexcites neuron A.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Hebb further proposed that storing something in short-term memory long enough made it possible for the brain to consolidate (strengthen) it into long-term memory, presumably by building new synapses or other structural changes.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If anything interrupted the rehearsal of short-term memory before consolidation completed its course, the information was simply lost.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-1-h06","text":"Our Changing Views of Consolidation"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"First, many short-term memories are not simply on their way to being long-term memories.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The original idea was that the brain held something in short-term memory until it could synthesize new proteins to establish a long-term memory.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"By that assumption, we should expect that consolidating a memory requires holding it in short-term memory for some fixed amount of time, presumably about the same in all cases.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, the time needed to form a long-term memory varies enormously.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The physiological explanation is that highly emotional experiences arouse the locus coeruleus, which increases norepinephrine release throughout the cortex and dopamine release in the hippocampus .","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Emotional experiences also increase the secretion of epinephrine and cortisol that activate the amygdala and hippocampus .","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Researchers call this the “synaptic tag-and-capture” process: Your brain tags a weak new memory for later stabilization if a similar, more important event soon follows it .","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-1-h07","text":"Working Memory"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"To improve the concept of short-term memory, A.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Hitch introduced the term working memory to refer to the way we store information while we are working with it.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One way to test working memory is the delayed response task , in which you respond to something that you saw or heard a short while ago.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Imagine that while you stare at a central fixation point, a light flashes briefly near the periphery.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"During the delay, cells in the prefrontal and parietal cortex increase their activity, and different cells become active depending on the direction the eye movement will need to take .","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"During any type of working memory task, a reverberating circuit holds the information, as Hebb had surmised.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The information reverberates among neighboring cells in the cortex and between the cerebral cortex and the thalamus .","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, cells holding an item in working memory do not simply repeat the stimulus.","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-1-h08","text":"Memory Loss"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In many cases, forgetting is a “feature,” not a “bug” .","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One likely hypothesis is that we need to forget outdated information to replace it with new information.","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, although some forgetting is good, you do not want to forget important or current information.","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One cause of amnesia is “brain fog” that many patients suffer for months after recovery from COVID-19 or from cancer treatments.","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Brain fog is marked by periods of forgetfulness, confusion, slow thinking, and impaired concentration.","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One hypothesis for brain fog is that the COVID virus causes a powerful reaction by the immune system that produces enough inflammatory cytokines to damage the blood-brain barrier and activate microglia cells that damage neurons and axons .","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Another hypothesis is that the reaction to the virus impairs the blood flow to the brain .","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Two patients with damage in the occipital cortex lost the ability to form new visual memories, such as the ability to recognize something seen a few moments ago, despite satisfactory memory in other ways .","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Two other patients could answer questions like, “Is a library quiet?” but not a question like, “Which is quiet, a concert","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-1-h09","text":"Alzheimer’s Disease"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sometimes they surprise themselves with their skilled performance because they don’t remember doing it before .","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Alzheimer’s disease gradually progresses to confusion, depression, apathy, hallucinations, delusions, sleeplessness, and loss of appetite.","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The first major clue to the cause of Alzheimer’s was the observation that most people with Down syndrome get Alzheimer’s disease if they survive into middle age .","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This gene makes a protein that contributes to many functions, including lipid metabolism and control of the blood-brain barrier.","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The APOE4 gene and at least two other genes are linked to many cases of early-onset Alzheimer’s disease .","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Type 2 diabetes is also a major risk factor, because insulin activity in the brain is important for storing memories .","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although most scientists believe it is one of the causes of Alzheimer’s, a minority opinion is that a small amount of b -amyloid might be the brain’s effort to protect itself .","sourcePrintedPage":391,"sourcePdfPage":409,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many scientists have expressed reservations because the benefits of the drug are uncertain, the side effects are serious, and the cost is high.","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"An important limitation is that Alzheimer’s relates to high levels of both b -amyloid and tau, so attacking just b -amyloid is not enough .","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-1-h10","text":"Infant Amnesia"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Infant amnesia (or early childhood amnesia) is not a disorder.","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It is the universal experience that older children and adults remember little of what happened in their first few years.","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"We keep the skills that we learned then, but we forget most or all the episodic memories.","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sigmund Freud may have been the first to call attention to this phenomenon.","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"His explanation was that children repress their early memories because of their association with severe sexual conflicts.","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Three- and four-year-olds, and even some two-year-olds, can accurately describe their last birthday party, their last visit to Grandma’s house, or other events from months ago .","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m12-1-h11","text":"In Closing: Memory and Forgetting"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Today, we distinguish among several types of learning and memory that rely on multiple mechanisms and multiple brain areas.","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"We learn about these mechanisms by studying forgetting as well as by studying learning.","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Early in life, for mice as for humans, the hippocampus rapidly forms new neurons and replaces old ones with new ones.","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In contrast to mice and humans, guinea pigs are relatively mature at birth, already walking around and eating solid food.","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Furthermore, chemical procedures that interfere with formation of new neurons impair both learning and forgetting in infant mice .","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Even later in life, procedures that increase the formation of new neurons in the hippocampus have been demonstrated to increase rats’ forgetting .","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"bullet","text":"For example, if a rat experiences a CS paired with shock, the shock elicits screaming and jumping, but the CS elicits a freezing response.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":384,"sourcePdfPage":402},{"type":"bullet","text":"In instrumental conditioning (also known as operant conditioning), a response leads to a reinforcer or punishment.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":384,"sourcePdfPage":402},{"type":"bullet","text":"The song that he heard was not paired with any other stimulus, so it doesn’t look like classical conditioning.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":386,"sourcePdfPage":404},{"type":"bullet","text":"In most situations, learning occurs only if the CS and UCS, or response and reinforcer, occur close together in time.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":386,"sourcePdfPage":404},{"type":"bullet","text":"Pavlov proposed that classical conditioning reflects a strengthened connection between a CS center and a UCS center in the brain that lets excitation of the CS center flow to the UCS center, evoking a response just like the unconditioned response.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":386,"sourcePdfPage":404},{"type":"bullet","text":"Regardless, Lashley’s results shared that at least some types of learning did not depend on connections across the cortex.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":386,"sourcePdfPage":404},{"type":"bullet","text":"Note, however, another interpretation of Lashley’s results: Maze learning and visual discrimination learning are complex tasks in which a rat attends to visual and tactile stimuli, the location of its body, the position of its head, and other cues.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405},{"type":"bullet","text":"At first, a rabbit closed its eye in response to the air puff but not the tone.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405},{"type":"bullet","text":"Damaging any of those areas will impair or eliminate the learned response, but we cannot be sure that learning occurred in the damaged area.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405},{"type":"bullet","text":"Damage in E or F will prevent learning by blocking the output from D.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405},{"type":"bullet","text":"If so, then D has to be active at the time of the learning, and so do the areas leading up to D (A, B, and C).","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":387,"sourcePdfPage":405},{"type":"bullet","text":"You can repeat something you just heard, and you can also describe something you experienced years ago.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":388,"sourcePdfPage":406},{"type":"bullet","text":"Hebb could not imagine a physical or chemical process that is fast enough to account for immediate memory yet stable enough for permanent memory.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":388,"sourcePdfPage":406},{"type":"bullet","text":"When you watch a soccer or hockey match, you remember the score until it changes.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h06","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407},{"type":"bullet","text":"If you park your car, your memory of its location is neither a short-term memory that fades within seconds, nor a memory that will last for years.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h06","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407},{"type":"bullet","text":"Flashbulb memories have a further aspect: Suppose you are driving on snow and you skid on a slippery patch.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h06","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407},{"type":"bullet","text":"Now you form a long-term memory of not only the accident but also the earlier slip.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h06","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407},{"type":"bullet","text":"You continue staring at the central point until you hear a beep, and then you are supposed to look to where you remember seeing the light.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h07","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407},{"type":"bullet","text":"Ordinarily, the brain’s representation of a visual image decays quickly, but if you need to remember the stimulus to respond to it later, activity in the visual cortex persists.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h07","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407},{"type":"bullet","text":"You want to remember where you are supposed to go at 11 o’clock tomorrow morning, and you don’t want to confuse that information with your appointment at 9 o’clock three weeks ago.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408},{"type":"bullet","text":"Sometimes amnesia is limited to a certain aspect of memory.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408},{"type":"bullet","text":"Here we briefly consider Alzheimer’s disease and the phenomenon of infant amnesia.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408},{"type":"bullet","text":"The second module considers amnesia resulting from damage to the hippocampus.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408},{"type":"bullet","text":"Daniel Schacter (1983) reported playing golf with an Alzheimer’s patient who remembered the rules and jargon of the game correctly but kept forgetting how many strokes he took.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408},{"type":"bullet","text":"People with one copy of the type 4 gene ( APOE4 ) have four times the normal risk of Alzheimer’s, and people with two copies have 15 times the normal risk.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":390,"sourcePdfPage":408},{"type":"bullet","text":"They also damage axons and dendrites, causing them to cluster into structures called plaques, as Figures 12.6 and 12.7 show.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":391,"sourcePdfPage":409},{"type":"bullet","text":"Many old people have high levels of b -amyloid without Alzheimer’s disease, and some have Alzheimer’s disease without especially high levels of b -amyloid.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":391,"sourcePdfPage":409},{"type":"bullet","text":"Pharmaceutical companies have made many attempts to alleviate Alzheimer’s by drugs that counteract b -amyloid, without much success.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410},{"type":"bullet","text":"Another explanation for the ineffectiveness of drugs so far is that the damage associated with Alzheimer’s may already be too extensive by the time the condition is diagnosed.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410},{"type":"bullet","text":"Later psychologists have offered explanations of why young children fail to form long-term memories, but in fact young children do form long-term memories.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h10","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410},{"type":"bullet","text":"Decades ago, Karl Lashley supposed that the physiology of learning might be a simple matter of increasing a single pathway in the cortex.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h11","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410},{"type":"bullet","text":"Hypotheses have included the development of language, or a sense of self, or complex reasoning abilities as children grow older.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h11","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410},{"type":"bullet","text":"Rats in their first weeks of life learn and retain their learning for a day or more, but they soon forget.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h11","sourcePrintedPage":392,"sourcePdfPage":410},{"type":"bullet","text":"Lashley sought to find the engram, the physiological representation of learning.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h11","sourcePrintedPage":393,"sourcePdfPage":411},{"type":"bullet","text":"Donald Hebb reasoned that no one mechanism could account for all the phenomena of learning.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":388,"sourcePdfPage":406},{"type":"bullet","text":"First, many short-term memories are not simply on their way to being long-term memories.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407},{"type":"bullet","text":"Hitch introduced the term working memory to refer to the way we store information while we are working with it.","headingId":"bp14-m12-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":389,"sourcePdfPage":407}],"topicIds":["bp14-m12-1-h01","bp14-m12-1-h02","bp14-m12-1-h03","bp14-m12-1-h04","bp14-m12-1-h05","bp14-m12-1-h06","bp14-m12-1-h07","bp14-m12-1-h08","bp14-m12-1-h09","bp14-m12-1-h10","bp14-m12-1-h11"],"studySections":[{"id":"bp14-m12-1-study-1","title":"Memory is not one storage box","text":"Learning can change behavior, but memory includes several kinds of information and different neural processes. Short-term retention, working memory, and long-term remembering differ in duration and functional demands. Working memory involves actively maintaining and using information for a current task. Long-term memory includes different forms, such as recalling events or gradually acquiring skills. The possibility that someone can lose one kind of memory while retaining another shows why the word 'memory' should not be treated as a single ability.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":384,"sourcePrintedEnd":394,"sourcePdfStart":402,"sourcePdfEnd":412},{"id":"bp14-m12-1-study-2","title":"The search for where memories are stored","text":"Early researchers, including Lashley, investigated whether memories occupy sharply localized brain sites. Results challenged the view that one tiny cortical location contains an entire learned response. Modern approaches investigate distributed neuronal populations and the ways training changes their connectivity. An engram refers to the physical changes underlying a memory, but identifying neurons active during learning is not by itself proof that they constitute the whole memory. Representations may involve several brain regions and time-dependent changes.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":384,"sourcePrintedEnd":394,"sourcePdfStart":402,"sourcePdfEnd":412},{"id":"bp14-m12-1-study-3","title":"Consolidation and forgetting","text":"Memories can change after initial learning through consolidation, retrieval, and reconsolidation-related processes. This means the formation of a lasting memory is not simply a one-time filing operation. Forgetting can arise through different mechanisms, including disrupted acquisition, storage, or retrieval. Stress, context, and brain damage may affect these processes differently. When interpreting a memory test, ask what type of learning was required and whether the person could express the information in another way.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":384,"sourcePrintedEnd":394,"sourcePdfStart":402,"sourcePdfEnd":412},{"id":"bp14-m12-1-study-4","title":"Clinical patterns","text":"Alzheimer's disease is associated with progressive changes in cognitive function and neural pathology, but memory difficulties alone do not establish that diagnosis. Infant amnesia refers to the limited ability adults have to recall early childhood autobiographical episodes; it does not mean infants are incapable of learning. Such examples demonstrate that memory is constrained by brain development, neural health, and the kind of information being assessed.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":384,"sourcePrintedEnd":394,"sourcePdfStart":402,"sourcePdfEnd":412}],"contentLevel":"complete_sample_classroom_notes_plus_legacy_source_extraction","selfCheck":[{"question":"Can you explain: Memory is not one storage box?","answer":"Learning can change behavior, but memory includes several kinds of information and different neural processes.
